title: Job, facts, limits
summary: Learn to brief a machine like a boss: ask one real question badly and well, check what came back against something you can test yourself, then debate whether a computer's word deserves belief.
materials: laptop or tablet with a chatbot, a grown-up signed in and nearby
the two-LED meeting machine from Think

steps.title: Brief the machine like a boss
steps.body:
This week you taught a robot with data. Today you learn to brief a different machine, a chatbot, and briefing is a speaking skill.

A weak ask is a mumble: the machine cannot see your desk, your week or your reasons, so it fills every hole with guesses. A strong ask has three parts you can count on your fingers. The job: exactly what you want back, a list, a plan, one number, three sentences. The facts: everything it needs that only you know. The limits: what it must not do, assume or skip.

One more thing before you type a word. Whatever comes back will be a claim, and week 1 taught you that claims come in two kinds: the kind you can check yourself and the kind you take on someone's word. A chatbot's answer does not stop being a claim just because it arrives instantly and sounds sure. The philosophy question of the week is: how do you know what a machine tells you is true? Today you answer it with your hands, not your feelings.

Voice rules, as always: speak to the back wall, pause after the sentence that matters most, look at one person per sentence.

steps.title: One question, asked twice
steps.body:
Your real question today is one you already own: when will the two LEDs flash in the same second?

First ask it badly on purpose. Type: when do the lights blink together? Read the answer with a straight face and copy its key claims onto the whiteboard.

Now ask it well. Job: list the exact seconds in the first minute when both LEDs flash in the same second, and show how you found them. Facts: one LED flashes on every third second, the other on every fourth, and both counts start together at zero. Limits: use only these facts, and if something is missing, say so instead of guessing. Type it as one clear message and copy the new answer beside the first.

Stand back and compare the two columns like a scientist. What did the machine have to invent when your facts were missing? Which of the three parts, job, facts or limits, was the weak ask missing most? Say the difference out loud in one sentence.
checklist: Both asks were sent, and both answers stand side by side on the whiteboard
I named at least one thing the machine guessed at when my facts were missing
I said which of job, facts and limits the weak ask lacked most
My strong ask fits in one message a stranger could act on

steps.title: The check
steps.body:
The strong answer claims some seconds. Which kind of claim is that: check it yourself, or take its word? You worked the true answer out in Think, and the meeting machine is sitting right there.

Check it twice. Against your own math first: do the machine's seconds match the meetings you found? Then against the copper: power the blinkers, count the drumbeats out loud, and catch a shared flash with your own eyes.

Now feel the other kind. Ask the chatbot something from this week you cannot test from your chair, like how many AA batteries the world makes in a year. Sort that answer into week 1's columns: whose word would you be taking, and how might they know? Finish by saying the difference between today's two answers out loud: one wore a claim you could corner, and one asked for trust.
checklist: The machine's seconds matched my math, or I found the mismatch and named it
I caught at least one shared flash live on the meeting machine
I sorted the untestable answer into the take-someone's-word column and said whose word
I can say which of today's two answers I trust more, and why

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record 90 seconds: read the weak ask and one line of its answer, read the strong ask and one line of its answer, name what changed using the words job, facts and limits, and close with your own answer to the question: how do you know what a machine tells you is true?
